title: How to Export Shopify Store Product Data to CSV or JSON
metaTitle: Export Shopify Store Product Data to CSV or JSON
metaDescription: Export any Shopify store's products, prices, variants and images to CSV or JSON from its public products.json, including stores you do not own.
summary: Give the ActorForge Shopify Store Scraper a store URL, let it page through the public products.json feed, then download the dataset as CSV or JSON or load it into pandas.
intro: If you own a Shopify store, the admin has a product CSV export. If you want the catalog of a competitor, a supplier or a store you are about to migrate, you do not have that option. What most Shopify stores do have is a public products.json feed: the same JSON catalog Shopify serves to every visitor, 250 products per page.

Paging through it yourself is doable for one store, but handling robots.txt, pacing, collections, headless storefronts that do not serve the feed, and turning nested JSON into a clean table quickly adds up. The [Shopify Store Scraper](actor:shopify-store-scraper) does that and returns one row per product with prices, compare-at prices, discount, stock, variants and images.
This guide walks through checking a store, choosing what to export, running the export and getting the result into CSV, JSON or pandas.

steps.name: Check that the store serves products.json
steps.text: Open https://the-store-domain/products.json in a browser. If you see JSON with a products array, the store works. Headless storefronts built on Hydrogen/Oxygen or a custom frontend do not serve it, and a few large brands block automated requests; the actor returns a free row explaining why in those cases, so you can also just try it.

steps.name: Add the store and choose the mode
steps.text: Put the store domain or any URL from the store in `storeUrls`; the actor takes the host, so a collection or product URL works too, as do myshopify.com domains. Keep `mode` as products for one row per product. Use both if you also want a single store summary row with product counts, price stats, theme and detected apps.

steps.name: Decide on scope and row size
steps.text: `maxProductsPerStore` defaults to 1,000 and goes up to 100,000; raise it for large catalogs. Use `collections` with handles such as mens-shoes to export only certain collections. `includeVariants` is on by default and adds every variant with SKU, price, compare-at price, availability, options and weight. Turn on `includeBodyHtml` only if you need product descriptions, because it makes rows much bigger (the price stays the same).

steps.name: Download the dataset as CSV or JSON
steps.text: When the run finishes, its dataset can be downloaded from Apify Console or the API in CSV, JSON and other formats. Use the `fields` parameter to choose a tidy set of columns for a spreadsheet, and request JSON when you want the nested variants and images kept intact.

code.code:
# Export the dataset of a finished run as CSV or JSON
DATASET_ID="your-dataset-id"

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.apify.com/v2/datasets/$DATASET_ID/items?format=csv&clean=true&fields=store,title,vendor,productType,price,priceMax,compareAtPriceMin,discountPct,currency,available,variantCount,updatedAt,url" \
  -o products.csv

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.apify.com/v2/datasets/$DATASET_ID/items?format=json&clean=true" \
  -o products.json

steps.name: Load it into pandas for a quick summary
steps.text: For analysis, read the product rows into a DataFrame, write the columns you need to CSV and summarize per store. The dataset can mix product and store rows in both mode, so filter on `type`.

code.code:
import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("actor-forge/shopify-store-scraper").call(run_input={
    "storeUrls": ["allbirds.com", "tentree.com"],
    "mode": "products",
    "maxProductsPerStore": 1000,
})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
products = pd.DataFrame([r for r in rows if r.get("type") == "product"])

cols = ["store", "title", "vendor", "productType", "price", "priceMax",
        "compareAtPriceMin", "discountPct", "currency", "available",
        "variantCount", "updatedAt", "url"]
products[cols].to_csv("shopify_products.csv", index=False)

# Quick per-store summary
summary = products.groupby("store").agg(
    products=("title", "count"),
    medianPrice=("price", "median"),
    onSaleShare=("onSale", "mean"),
    inStockShare=("available", "mean"),
)
print(summary)

steps.name: Keep the export fresh with updatedSince
steps.text: For an ongoing price and stock feed, schedule the same input daily and set `updatedSince` to the previous day's date (YYYY-MM-DD) or an ISO timestamp. Only products whose updated_at is on or after that moment become rows, and skipped products are never charged, so you can merge each day's changes into your master export.

sampleOutputNote: Product rows come out like this, with price, compare-at price, discount and stock in the first columns:
costExample: Product rows cost $0.0003 each, so exporting a 1,000-product store is $0.30 and three such stores are $0.90. In both mode, each store row adds $0.005, so the same three stores with summaries cost $0.915.
tips: products.json only lists published products. Drafts, archived items and inventory quantities are not public, and prices are the store's base-currency prices, not market-specific or B2B prices.
In both mode, check `catalogComplete` on the store row: it tells you whether the stats cover the whole catalog or were cut off by `maxProductsPerStore`.
The actor obeys each store's robots.txt and Crawl-delay and runs about 1.3 requests per second per store, so very large catalogs take a while. Several stores run in parallel, up to 3 at a time.
A 401, 403, 429 or bot challenge stops that store immediately with no retries. Those rows are free, but the store's products will be missing from the export.

faq.q: Can I export products from a Shopify store I don't own?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the store serves Shopify's public products.json feed and its robots.txt allows it. The actor reads only that public catalog data and no customer or contact data.

faq.q: Does the export include product images?
faq.a: Yes. Each product row includes every image URL plus a featured image. The files themselves are not downloaded; you get the URLs.

faq.q: Why does my CSV have fewer products than the store's website shows?
faq.a: Common reasons are the `maxProductsPerStore` cap (default 1,000), a `collections` filter, an `updatedSince` filter, or products that are not published. Raise the cap and clear the filters for a full export.

faq.q: Can I export several stores in one run?
faq.a: Yes. Add them all to `storeUrls`; duplicates are removed and each row carries a `store` column, so one CSV can hold several catalogs.
